Heating and AC Help Across Greater Houston

One free number for Houston and its suburbs in Harris, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Brazoria and Galveston counties. Find your town below, or call and say where you are.

Call (832) 662-4107 Find your town
  1. Home
  2. Service Areas

The line takes heating and air conditioning calls from the City of Houston and the suburbs around it. Each town below has its own page about what is different there: how old the houses are, which utility owns the wires, how flooding and storms have hit, and who handles permits.

How coverage works: an automated assistant answers (832) 662-4107 at any hour, asks where you are and what the heating or cooling is doing, and passes the call to a separately owned local HVAC business serving the Houston area. The line has no office in any of these towns and does not send anyone itself. The company you reach decides whether it can take the job, prices it and does the work.

Find your town

Grouped by side of town. Each link opens a page written for that place.

North: Montgomery County and north Harris County

  • The Woodlands Planned forest community opened in 1974 and run by a township, spanning Montgomery and Harris counties.
  • Spring Unincorporated railroad town from 1871, now a Harris County community of about 62,500 people with no city government.
  • Humble Small city born in a 1905 oil boom beside Bush Intercontinental, ringed by larger unincorporated areas such as Atascocita near Lake Houston.
  • Kingwood Wooded master planned community on Lake Houston, part of the City of Houston since its annexation in the mid 1990s.
  • Conroe Montgomery County seat near Lake Conroe, with an estimated 114,581 residents in July 2024, about 27 percent above its 2020 count.
  • Tomball Northwest Harris County city of 12,341 in 2020, founded as a 1907 rail town, with its own city owned natural gas system.

West and northwest

  • Cypress Unincorporated northwest Harris County community along US 290 that stayed rural until the 1980s, now one of the area's largest suburbs.
  • Katy Former rice and railroad town spanning Harris, Fort Bend and Waller counties, inside a much larger suburban Katy area.
  • Fulshear Western Fort Bend County city that grew from 1,134 people in 2010 to an estimated 64,630 in 2025, mostly in new homes.

Southwest: Fort Bend County

  • Sugar Land Former sugar company town incorporated in 1959, with 111,026 residents in 2020 and many neighborhoods inside levee districts.
  • Missouri City Fort Bend city incorporated in 1956, mixing 1970s Quail Valley homes with newer planned communities.
  • Richmond Fort Bend County seat on the Brazos River, founded in 1837 and home to 11,627 people in 2020.
  • Fresno Unincorporated Fort Bend County community of 24,486 in 2020 with no city hall, so county rules apply.

South and the bay: Brazoria and Galveston counties

  • Pearland Mostly Brazoria County city that grew from 37,640 people in 2000 to 125,828 in 2020.
  • League City Fast growing Galveston County suburb near Clear Lake and NASA, where electricity may come from TNMP or CenterPoint.
  • Friendswood Galveston and Harris County city founded by Quakers in 1895, a NASA era suburb that flooded badly in Harvey.

East: the Ship Channel and Baytown

  • Pasadena Ship Channel city founded in 1893 whose refinery driven postwar boom left about half its homes built before 1977.
  • Baytown Oil and refinery city formed in 1948 from Goose Creek, Pelly and Baytown, on Galveston Bay at the east edge of Harris County.

Cities, townships and unincorporated areas

Greater Houston mixes three kinds of places, and the difference matters when equipment is replaced. Incorporated cities such as Houston, Sugar Land, Pearland, Katy and League City run their own permit offices. Kingwood is part of the City of Houston, so Houston's rules apply there. The Woodlands is governed by a township with its own residential design review. Cypress, Spring and Fresno have no city government at all.

You do not need to sort this out before you call. It helps to know it when you compare quotes for a replacement: ask each company whether a permit or design approval applies at your address, who obtains it, and whether the inspection is included.

Who owns the wires where you live

Power outages are common in Houston hurricane season, and a dead air conditioner during an outage is a utility problem, not an HVAC one. Across most of the area, CenterPoint Energy delivers electricity and you buy it from the retail provider you choose. Parts of Montgomery County, including Conroe and some neighborhoods of The Woodlands (which is split between two utilities), are on Entergy Texas lines, and much of Galveston County, including Friendswood and League City, is on TNMP lines. The company that delivers your power is printed on your bill, and that is who to call about an outage.

  2. Say what is wrongTell it whether the trouble is cooling or heating, where in the Houston area you are, and what the system is doing.
  3. Reach a local companyYour call is transferred to an independent, locally owned HVAC company, which gets a short summary of your problem before it answers.
  4. Work it out with themThat company inspects, quotes, repairs and bills you directly. If nobody can pick up, your name, number and problem are passed on for a call back.

Verify the license before work begins. Texas requires anyone contracting to do air conditioning, refrigeration or heating work to hold an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration (ACR) Contractor license from the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). Ask the company for its ACR license number, then confirm it on the TDLR license search (opens in a new tab). The line does not check this for you.

Common questions

Is there a Houston Air & Heating office near me?

There is not. It is only a phone number and this website: no offices, technicians or trucks anywhere. Your call goes to a separately owned local HVAC business serving the area. Ask that company directly whether it serves your street and when it can come out.

What if my suburb has no page here?

Call anyway if you live in greater Houston. The town pages cover places people search for most, not the edge of where calls are taken. Tell the assistant your city or ZIP code and it routes the call.

Do unincorporated areas like Cypress and Spring need a permit for a new AC?

Places without a city government do not have a city permit office, so whatever rules apply come from the county, the utility and any deed restrictions or homeowner association covenants. Rules differ by location, so ask the HVAC company what applies at your address and whether it will handle any required permit. Inside a city such as Houston, Sugar Land or Pearland, the city's permit rules apply.

The whole house lost power. Is that an AC problem?

Usually not. A whole-house outage is a job for the electric delivery company that owns the lines at your address, which is named on your electric bill. In most of the Houston area that is CenterPoint Energy; parts of Montgomery County, including parts of The Woodlands, are served by Entergy Texas, and much of Galveston County, including Friendswood and League City, by TNMP. Some neighborhoods are split, so check your bill. An HVAC company cannot restore power.

Anywhere around Houston, the same free call

One free call, any hour. Say whether it is the AC or the heat, where you are and what is happening, and the line transfers you to an independent, locally owned HVAC company that looks at the system and prices the job itself.

Houston Air & Heating is a free phone line, not an HVAC contractor. It answers your call and connects you with an independent local heating and air conditioning company, which inspects, quotes and does the work, and which you pay directly. Companies may pay a referral fee. You never pay the line.
